title: Nice to meet you
goal: Greet people, say your name and where you are from, ask how someone is — and set up two habits that differ from English from the very first sentence: the verb "to be" sits at the end, and so does every other verb.
bekal: greet people, welcome guests, and say goodbye
say your name, where you are from, and your nationality in full sentences
use the seven forms of "to be": یم، یې، دی، ده، یو، یاست، دي

dialogs.title: خبرې اترې — د کابل هوایي ډګر ته
dialogs.intro: Budi has just landed in Kabul. Someone is waiting for him at the exit, holding a sheet of paper with his name on it.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: And upon you be peace. Thank you very much.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: هو، زه بودي یم. ستاسو نوم څه دی؟
lines.baca: ho, zə Būdī yəm. stāso nūm tsə day?
lines.id: Yes, I'm Budi. What's your name?
lines.literal: yes, I Budi am. of-you(pl) name what is?

lines.speaker: نجیب:
lines.text: زما نوم نجیب دی. زه ستاسو ملګری یم.
lines.baca: zmā nūm Najīb day. zə stāso malgəray yəm.
lines.id: My name is Najib. I'm your friend.
lines.literal: of-me name Najib is. I of-you(pl) friend am.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Pleased to meet you, Mr. Najib.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: زه ښه یم، مننه. او تاسو؟
lines.baca: zə ṣa yəm, manana. aw tāso?
lines.id: I'm fine, thank you. And you?
lines.literal: I good am, thanks. and you(pl)?

lines.speaker: نجیب:
lines.text: زه هم ښه یم. تاسو له کوم ځایه یاست؟
lines.baca: zə ham ṣa yəm. tāso lə kūm dzāya yāst?
lines.id: I'm fine too. Where are you from?
lines.literal: I also good am. you(pl) from which place-from are?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: زه له اندونیزیا څخه یم. تاسو افغان یاست؟
lines.baca: zə lə Indonezyā tsəkha yəm. tāso afghān yāst?
lines.id: I'm from Indonesia. Are you Afghan?
lines.literal: I from Indonesia from am. you(pl) Afghan are?

lines.speaker: نجیب:
lines.text: هو، زه د کابل یم. دا زما خور ده، زرغونه.
lines.baca: ho, zə də Kābəl yəm. dā zmā khor da, Zarghūna.
lines.id: Yes, I'm from Kabul. This is my sister, Zarghuna.
lines.literal: yes, I of Kabul am. this of-me sister is, Zarghuna.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: مننه. کابل ډېر ښکلی ښار دی.
lines.baca: manana. Kābəl ḍer ṣkulay ṣār day.
lines.id: Thank you. Kabul is a very beautiful city.
lines.literal: thanks. Kabul very beautiful city is.

lines.speaker: نجیب:
lines.id: Come on, let's go. The car is outside.

notes: In Pashto the verb "to be" must be there, and it goes at the end of the sentence. English puts it in the middle — "I am Budi" — Pashto says زه بودي **یم**, "I Budi am". Two new habits arrive today at once, and both will come back in every unit until the last page.

Notice that "is" differs for men and women. Najib says هغه ډاکټر **دی** for a man, but زرغونه ډاکټره **ده** for a woman. This is not politeness but gender — and it will spread to adjectives, demonstratives, and verbs from unit 2 on.

The welcome greeting ښه راغلاست literally means "good (that) you came". It is used for guests who have just arrived, at home or at the airport, and the reply is simply مننه (thank you). The informal form for one person: ښه راغلې.

There are two words for thank you, and both are right. The native Pashto word is مننه *manana*; the borrowing from Persian and Arabic تشکر *tashakkur* is also widely used, especially in Kabul. Warmer: ډېره مننه (thank you very much). The reply: هېڅ خبره نشته *hets khabara nishta*, "it's nothing at all".

The polite form تاسو is used even to one person. With people you have just met, shopkeepers, older people, or anyone you are not close to, use تاسو and the ending ـئ. The informal ته is only for close friends your own age, younger siblings, and children. If in doubt, تاسو is never wrong.

The invitation راځئ means both "come on" and "come here". The phrase راځئ، ځو literally means "come (you), we go" — the invitation you will hear most often in Afghanistan, from getting into a car to sitting down to eat.

grammars.title: The seven forms of "to be"
body: Pashto has one verb "to be", and its form changes with who is speaking. The seven forms below cover all everyday conversation, and you will need them in every unit that follows.
Look at the third and fourth rows. For the third person singular, the form splits by gender: دی for a man, ده for a woman. English "is" makes no such choice; Pashto does.

grammars.title: The verb goes at the end — always
body: English builds a sentence as subject, verb, then object: "I read a book". Pashto moves the verb to the end: زه کتاب لولم, literally "I book read". This order never changes, and that is good news — once you are used to it, it works for every sentence.
Question words don't move anything. Unlike English, which swaps the verb around ("Where are you?"), Pashto leaves the order intact and simply puts the question word where the answer will later stand.

head: Pashto
Say it
When to use it
rows: The most common greeting in Afghanistan, any time, to anyone.
The short form. Casual, used among friends and on the phone.
Welcome — to a guest who has just arrived.
Good morning. Literally "your morning with goodness".
How are you? The safest form.
Have a good trip — to someone leaving.
See you again. Casual and warm.

blocks.text: Two words for "you", and how to choose
Pashto makes you choose a level of politeness in every sentence, and the choice carries through to the verb ending. For now one rule is enough, and you will never offend anyone.

head: Form
To whom
Its verbs
rows: **Always use this.** New people, older people, bosses, shopkeepers, anyone you are not close to — even if it is just one person.
Close friends your own age, younger siblings, children, and in prayer.

blocks.title: If in doubt, use تاسو — it costs you nothing
items: Using تاسو with a close friend only sounds a little stiff, and they will laugh and tell you to use ته. Using ته with someone you have just met sounds dismissive, and nobody will correct you — they will simply keep their distance.
The switch from تاسو to ته is usually offered by the older person: ته ووایه *tə wowāya*, "just say *tə*". Wait for that offer.
The word صاحب *sāhib* after a man's name is a mark of respect that is never wrong: نجیب صاحب. For women, ښاغلې is used, or simply her name with تاسو.

blocks.title: Asking "yes or no" — just raise your voice
items: Pashto has no special word for making yes-no questions. The sentence تاسو افغان یاست (you are Afghan) becomes a question just by raising the pitch at the end: تاسو افغان یاست؟
Nothing is taken apart and no words swap places — unlike English "Are you…?". It is one of the things that make Pashto friendlier than it looks.
The answers: هو *ho* (yes) · نه *nə* (no) · ښایي *ṣāyī* (maybe) · هرومرو *harūmarū* (of course).
Look at the question mark: ؟ — it is a mirror image of the Latin one, because the script runs from right to left.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Pashto. Use the polite form (تاسو).
items: Peace be upon you! How are you?

exercises.prompt: Complete with the right form of "to be" (یم، یې، دی، ده، یو، یاست، دي).
Choose the right expression for each situation.
items: You greet a new neighbor in the morning.
You welcome a guest who has just arrived at your home.
You say goodbye as you leave a friend's house.
Your friend is about to leave for Kandahar.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order. Remember: the verb goes last.
